example: They all know they were told that it's all a bit above board.
correct_substitution: They all know they were told that it's all entirely legitimate and open.
explanation_correct: Above board means honest and without concealment.
incorrect_substitution: They all know they were told that it's all thoroughly underhand and secret.
explanation_incorrect: Above board means open and legitimate, but the sentence describes concealment.

example: Really it's only a few miles as the crow flies.
correct_substitution: Really it's only a few miles measured in a straight line.
explanation_correct: As the crow flies means the direct distance, ignoring the winding route.
incorrect_substitution: Really it's only a few miles measured along every twist of the road.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means straight-line distance, but the sentence describes the winding route.

example: Beggars can't be choosers, wherever we've got to take it.
correct_substitution: People in need cannot be fussy, wherever we've got to take it.
explanation_correct: The saying means those dependent on others must accept what is offered.
incorrect_substitution: People in need can demand exactly what they want, wherever we've got to take it.
explanation_incorrect: The saying denies the needy any choice, but the sentence grants them full demands.

example: I'm caught betwixt and between, which do I like the best.
correct_substitution: I'm caught in an undecided middle position, which do I like the best.
explanation_correct: Betwixt and between means being in an indeterminate state between two options.
incorrect_substitution: I'm caught firmly on one settled side, which do I like the best.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being undecided, but the sentence describes a firm choice, which the question contradicts.

example: You cannot wear silver studs and a bleeding heart on the same sleeve.
correct_substitution: You cannot wear silver studs and showy sentimental compassion on the same sleeve.
explanation_correct: A bleeding heart means ostentatious and excessive sympathy for others.
incorrect_substitution: You cannot wear silver studs and cold hard indifference on the same sleeve.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means excessive compassion, but the sentence describes callousness.

example: Why doesn't it have a mark on it for absolute brass monkey weather?
correct_substitution: Why doesn't it have a mark on it for bitterly freezing weather?
explanation_correct: Brass monkey weather means extremely cold conditions.
incorrect_substitution: Why doesn't it have a mark on it for swelteringly hot weather?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means extreme cold, but the sentence describes heat.

example: That's completely gone by the by.
correct_substitution: That's become completely beside the point.
explanation_correct: By the by means incidental and no longer relevant to the matter.
incorrect_substitution: That's become completely central to the point.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being incidental, but the sentence makes it the main issue.

idiom: by the seat of your pants
example: Just going in and sort of flying by the seat of your pants.
correct_substitution: Just going in and sort of improvising without any plan.
explanation_correct: By the seat of your pants means acting on instinct without preparation.
incorrect_substitution: Just going in and sort of following a meticulous plan.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means improvising, but the sentence describes careful planning.

example: They say an Ulsterman calls a spade a spade.
correct_substitution: They say an Ulsterman speaks plainly and bluntly.
explanation_correct: To call a spade a spade means to speak frankly without softening language.
incorrect_substitution: They say an Ulsterman speaks in careful euphemisms.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means blunt speech, but the sentence describes evasive wording.

example: If they all came up trumps that's Nottinghamshire covered basically.
correct_substitution: If they all delivered better than expected that's Nottinghamshire covered basically.
explanation_correct: To come up trumps means to produce a good result when it is needed.
incorrect_substitution: If they all failed badly that's Nottinghamshire covered basically.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means succeeding when needed, but the sentence describes failure, which would cover nothing.

example: It's duck soup for someone of her sort to find a new companion.
correct_substitution: It's extremely easy for someone of her sort to find a new companion.
explanation_correct: Duck soup means something requiring almost no effort.
incorrect_substitution: It's extremely difficult for someone of her sort to find a new companion.
explanation_incorrect: Duck soup means something easy, but the sentence describes difficulty.

example: What would they do without the eternal triangle?
correct_substitution: What would they do without the recurring three-person love rivalry?
explanation_correct: The eternal triangle refers to the perennial dramatic situation of two people competing for a third.
incorrect_substitution: What would they do without the simple contented couple?
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means a three-way romantic rivalry, but the sentence describes an untroubled pair.

example: Interest costs continue to fall in line with reduced borrowing.
correct_substitution: Interest costs continue to fall in proportion with reduced borrowing.
explanation_correct: To fall in line with something means to move in step or proportion with it.
incorrect_substitution: Interest costs continue to fall in complete opposition to reduced borrowing.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means moving in proportion, but the sentence describes moving contrary to it.

idiom: fall off the back of a lorry
example: Did they fall off the back of a lorry?
correct_substitution: Were they obtained through dubious or stolen means?
explanation_correct: The idiom is a euphemism for goods that are stolen or of questionable origin.
incorrect_substitution: Were they obtained through fully documented legitimate purchase?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom implies dubious origin, but the sentence describes a lawful purchase.

example: That door was really getting on my wick.
correct_substitution: That door was really irritating me badly.
explanation_correct: To get on someone's wick means to annoy them persistently.
incorrect_substitution: That door was really pleasing me greatly.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means causing irritation, but the sentence describes pleasure.

example: I was being bossy last night and just couldn't hack it.
correct_substitution: I was being bossy last night and just couldn't cope with it.
explanation_correct: To hack it means to manage or endure a demanding situation.
incorrect_substitution: I was being bossy last night and just handled it effortlessly.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means coping, but the sentence describes managing with ease, which contradicts 'couldn't'.

example: We've got twenty or thirty girls back there going at it hammer and tongs.
correct_substitution: We've got twenty or thirty girls back there going at it with furious energy.
explanation_correct: Hammer and tongs means doing something with great vigour or fighting fiercely.
incorrect_substitution: We've got twenty or thirty girls back there going at it with listless calm.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means acting with fierce energy, but the sentence describes languor.

example: He just looks at me hard as nails.
correct_substitution: He just looks at me with utter unfeeling toughness.
explanation_correct: Hard as nails means being tough and showing no sympathy.
incorrect_substitution: He just looks at me with tender soft-hearted warmth.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being unfeeling, but the sentence describes warmth.

example: If I lose it, well, it's hard cheese.
correct_substitution: If I lose it, well, that's just bad luck.
explanation_correct: Hard cheese means unfortunate luck, said with resignation or little sympathy.
incorrect_substitution: If I lose it, well, that's just marvellous fortune.
explanation_incorrect: Hard cheese means bad luck, but the sentence describes good fortune.

example: So I said to myself, where shall I have a ball?
correct_substitution: So I said to myself, where shall I thoroughly enjoy myself?
explanation_correct: To have a ball means to have a very good time.
incorrect_substitution: So I said to myself, where shall I thoroughly miserable myself?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means enjoying yourself greatly, but the sentence describes seeking misery.

example: Gemma had not the heart to tell either of them how much they wearied her.
correct_substitution: Gemma lacked the willingness to tell either of them how much they wearied her.
explanation_correct: Not to have the heart to do something means to be unable to bring yourself to do it.
incorrect_substitution: Gemma had every eagerness to tell either of them how much they wearied her.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means being unable to bring yourself to act, but the sentence describes eagerness.

example: I swear you have a screw loose.
correct_substitution: I swear you are slightly mad.
explanation_correct: To have a screw loose means to be somewhat unhinged.
incorrect_substitution: I swear you are entirely rational.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being unhinged, but the sentence describes sound reasoning.

example: No doubt about it — Shelly had the hots for me.
correct_substitution: No doubt about it — Shelly was strongly attracted to me.
explanation_correct: To have the hots for someone means to feel strong physical attraction to them.
incorrect_substitution: No doubt about it — Shelly was completely indifferent to me.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means strong attraction, but the sentence describes indifference.

example: There's no question that when Jimmy decides enough he will hold a very firm line.
correct_substitution: There's no question that when Jimmy decides enough he will refuse to give ground.
explanation_correct: To hold the line means to maintain a position under pressure.
incorrect_substitution: There's no question that when Jimmy decides enough he will yield ground immediately.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means standing firm, but the sentence describes conceding.

example: That young man has put a woman in the family way.
correct_substitution: That young man has made a woman pregnant.
explanation_correct: In the family way is a dated euphemism for being pregnant.
incorrect_substitution: That young man has made a woman entirely childless.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means becoming pregnant, but the sentence describes the opposite.

example: He won't have the books in the works.
correct_substitution: He won't have the books already in preparation.
explanation_correct: In the works means being prepared or under way.
incorrect_substitution: He won't have the books already completed and finished.
explanation_incorrect: In the works means still in preparation, but the sentence describes something finished.

example: But for now, they are only the best kick-ass rock band in the country.
correct_substitution: But for now, they are only the most forcefully energetic rock band in the country.
explanation_correct: Kick-ass means aggressively impressive and full of force.
incorrect_substitution: But for now, they are only the most gentle and restrained rock band in the country.
explanation_incorrect: Kick-ass means forcefully energetic, but the sentence describes mildness.

example: Your daddy told you to knock it off now.
correct_substitution: Your daddy told you to stop that at once now.
explanation_correct: To knock it off means to cease an annoying behaviour.
incorrect_substitution: Your daddy told you to carry on with that now.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means stopping, but the sentence encourages continuing.

example: You'd been asleep, you were not in the land of nod at all.
correct_substitution: You'd been asleep, you were not in the state of slumber at all.
explanation_correct: The land of nod means the state of being asleep.
incorrect_substitution: You'd been asleep, you were not wide awake at all.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means being asleep, but the sentence substitutes wakefulness, contradicting the first clause.

example: I thought to myself, perhaps he might lend me a hand?
correct_substitution: I thought to myself, perhaps he might give me some help?
explanation_correct: To lend a hand means to assist someone.
incorrect_substitution: I thought to myself, perhaps he might obstruct me entirely?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means helping, but the sentence describes hindrance.

example: Let's be having you! he grumbled, impatiently donning his top hat.
correct_substitution: Come along and get moving! he grumbled, impatiently donning his top hat.
explanation_correct: Let's be having you is a brisk call for someone to hurry up.
incorrect_substitution: Take all the time you need! he grumbled, impatiently donning his top hat.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase urges haste, but the sentence invites delay, which the impatience contradicts.

example: Now that the men of straw are men of plastic.
correct_substitution: Now that the insubstantial figureheads are men of plastic.
explanation_correct: A man of straw means someone without real substance or authority.
incorrect_substitution: Now that the genuinely powerful leaders are men of plastic.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means an insubstantial figure, but the sentence describes real power.

example: Never you mind them, they'll hear what you've got to say sooner or later.
correct_substitution: Pay no attention to them, they'll hear what you've got to say sooner or later.
explanation_correct: Never you mind means to disregard something as not your concern.
incorrect_substitution: Watch them very closely, they'll hear what you've got to say sooner or later.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase means disregarding something, but the sentence urges close attention.

example: One, two, three on the bounce.
correct_substitution: One, two, three in unbroken succession.
explanation_correct: On the bounce means occurring consecutively without a break.
incorrect_substitution: One, two, three at widely scattered intervals.
explanation_incorrect: On the bounce means consecutive, but the sentence describes wide separation.

example: Intensely junipery on the nose with a hint of sweetness.
correct_substitution: Intensely junipery in its aroma with a hint of sweetness.
explanation_correct: On the nose in tasting means how something smells.
incorrect_substitution: Intensely junipery in its aftertaste with a hint of sweetness.
explanation_incorrect: On the nose refers to smell, but the sentence describes taste after swallowing.

example: Is she out on the pull tonight?
correct_substitution: Is she out looking for a romantic partner tonight?
explanation_correct: On the pull means actively seeking a sexual or romantic partner.
incorrect_substitution: Is she out avoiding all company tonight?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means seeking a partner, but the sentence describes shunning company.

example: Anybody gets out of line, we just run him clear off the island.
correct_substitution: Anybody behaves unacceptably, we just run him clear off the island.
explanation_correct: Out of line means behaving in a way that breaches accepted limits.
incorrect_substitution: Anybody behaves impeccably, we just run him clear off the island.
explanation_incorrect: Out of line means misbehaving, but the sentence punishes good conduct.

example: Yeah well that's par for the course.
correct_substitution: Yeah well that's exactly what you would expect.
explanation_correct: Par for the course means something is typical and unsurprising.
incorrect_substitution: Yeah well that's utterly astonishing and unheard of.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means something typical, but the sentence describes it as extraordinary.

example: Passing the time of day about things in general.
correct_substitution: Exchanging brief pleasantries about things in general.
explanation_correct: To pass the time of day means to make casual small talk.
incorrect_substitution: Conducting intense formal negotiations about things in general.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means casual chat, but the sentence describes serious negotiation.

example: Someone else is playing the same game — following him with a series of cars.
correct_substitution: Someone else is engaged in the same manipulative behaviour — following him with a series of cars.
explanation_correct: To play games means to behave deviously rather than straightforwardly.
incorrect_substitution: Someone else is engaged in the same open honesty — following him with a series of cars.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means acting deviously, but the sentence describes transparency, which covert following contradicts.

example: Coons has started working out daily in a pumping iron gym.
correct_substitution: Coons has started working out daily in a weightlifting gym.
explanation_correct: To pump iron means to lift weights for exercise.
incorrect_substitution: Coons has started working out daily in a quiet meditation gym.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means weightlifting, but the sentence describes a sedentary activity.

example: Seeing is believing … the videophone which takes the blind out of date.
correct_substitution: Direct sight convinces where description cannot … the videophone which takes the blind out of date.
explanation_correct: Seeing is believing means visual evidence is more convincing than any account.
incorrect_substitution: Direct sight convinces no one at all … the videophone which takes the blind out of date.
explanation_incorrect: The saying holds that seeing convinces, but the sentence denies it, which the videophone contradicts.

example: We decided that we would split the difference between the two figures.
correct_substitution: We decided that we would settle midway between the two figures.
explanation_correct: To split the difference means to compromise at the midpoint between two positions.
incorrect_substitution: We decided that we would insist on the extreme end of the two figures.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means compromising midway, but the sentence describes refusing to move.

example: He doesn't come and whisper sweet nothings in our ears.
correct_substitution: He doesn't come and whisper affectionate trifles in our ears.
explanation_correct: Sweet nothings means endearments of no real content, murmured affectionately.
incorrect_substitution: He doesn't come and whisper harsh criticisms in our ears.
explanation_incorrect: Sweet nothings means affectionate murmurings, but the sentence describes rebukes.

example: If at any stage you want to talk turkey.
correct_substitution: If at any stage you want to discuss matters frankly and seriously.
explanation_correct: To talk turkey means to get down to serious, plain-speaking discussion.
incorrect_substitution: If at any stage you want to discuss matters vaguely and evasively.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means frank discussion, but the sentence describes evasion.

example: Okay, third time lucky.
correct_substitution: Okay, this third attempt should be the one that succeeds.
explanation_correct: Third time lucky expresses hope that a third attempt will succeed after two failures.
incorrect_substitution: Okay, this third attempt is certain to fail like the others.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase expresses hope of success, but the sentence predicts another failure.

example: Two proposals, with a view to reducing the rateable value of the flats.
correct_substitution: Two proposals, with the intention of reducing the rateable value of the flats.
explanation_correct: With a view to means having a particular purpose in mind.
incorrect_substitution: Two proposals, with no intention whatever of reducing the rateable value of the flats.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase states a purpose, but the sentence denies having one.
